column4: The sacrificial herd, guidance, and piety meet explicitly: neither flesh nor blood reaches God, but taqwa does, and the worshippers magnify Him for having guided them.
Spending to seek God's pleasure is pictured as a rain-fed upland garden that gives its crop twice over; this is the section's giver-tree, sought face, height, rain, and increase in one scene.
This ayah joins divine guidance to spending done only in seeking God's face and says the good spent returns to the giver, directly clarifying the motives and self-directed purification of 92:18-20.
The feeders say they give only for God's face and want neither recompense nor thanks; this is the clearest parallel to giving without a human favor that must be repaid.
The phrase فَمَا ٱسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ ٱلْهَدْىِ puts the source section's two dictionary branches together: y-s-r and the sacrificial animal called hady.
The Prophet is told to take charity from their wealth so that it cleanses and causes them to grow, staging both the collector and the purifying growth of the giver.
The command to give the crop's due on harvest day turns agricultural yield into an obligation of giving, exactly the harvest-right scene developed in the section.
Spending wealth in God's way is a seed growing seven ears with a hundred grains each, the Quran's explicit formulation of giving as crop multiplication.
The herd has جمال when driven home and sent out to pasture, supplying the section's named daily scene of desert wealth.
The recipients of alms explicitly include وَٱلْعَامِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا, the officials who collect them, corresponding to the dictionary sense of sāʿī as zakat collector.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ makes self-purification the condition of flourishing, the outcome enacted by the giver of 92:18.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّىٰهَا locates success in purifying the soul and supplies the immediately preceding surah's transitive counterpart to يَتَزَكَّىٰ.
Whoever purifies himself does so for his own soul, directly explaining how the wealth-giver's act increases and cleanses its giver rather than enriching God.
The sacrificial camels are signs of God, contain good, are slaughtered in His name, and feed both the contented and the petitioner; the herd becomes worship and provision for others.
Every community receives a rite in which God's name is spoken over the livestock He provided, placing ritual direction, gift, and بهيمة الأنعام in one frame.
A hunting penalty must be هَدْيًا بَٰلِغَ ٱلْكَعْبَةِ, an animal offering reaching the Kaaba, virtually the section's dictionary definition of hady brought to the sanctuary.
The hady is detained from reaching its place of sacrifice; this negative event makes the destination inherent in the source section's sense of هدي especially visible.
Sacrificial animals provide temporary benefits and then reach their appointed place at the Ancient House, joining useful herd wealth to its sacred destination.
Honoring God's sacrificial signs is said to arise from the piety of hearts, preparing the precise claim in 22:37 that taqwa, rather than meat or blood, reaches God.
Pilgrims name God over the livestock He provided, then eat and feed the destitute; a provided herd is turned into voluntary worship and sustenance.
The two sons offer sacrifices and acceptance is restricted to the God-fearing, a direct parallel to 22:37's insistence that the operative content of an offering is taqwa.
The command فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ directs sacrifice specifically to the Lord, matching the section's animal gift whose true orientation is the face of its Rabb.

Livestock contain pure, palatable milk drawn from within their bodies, supplying the concrete household substance behind the section's secondary senses of yusr and kadhaba as milk increasing or failing.
Livestock are a lesson: God gives drink from their bellies and places many benefits and food in them, directly presenting herd, milk, provision, and benefit together.
Humans are made owners of livestock God created for them, closely matching the section's opening identification of the desert household's property with its herd.
The livestock are subdued for riding and eating, showing how herd wealth is made fit for its owner.
The herd supplies benefits and drinks, completing the milk-and-wealth scene and calling for gratitude for the provision.
God creates livestock with warmth, benefits, and food for people; this establishes why anʿām can be the desert's māl and niʿma.
Tents from livestock hides and furnishings from wool, fur, and hair depict exactly how the herd constitutes the portable wealth of desert life.
God appoints livestock for riding and eating, explicitly presenting the herd as a divinely fitted provision.
Livestock yield benefits, carry people to needs in their breasts, and share the transport role of ships, expanding the practical content of herd wealth.
God makes pairs from humans and from livestock and multiplies creatures through them, joining male and female, herd, and increase in one formulation.
Human creation, eight livestock pairs, and formation in mothers' wombs are placed together under the one Lord, uniting the section's sexed earth, herd, womb, and gradual nurture.
Pairs of sheep and goats are questioned by male, female, and what the females' wombs contain, a literal herd counterpart to the section's male/female and reproductive imagery.
Pairs of camels and cattle are likewise tested against male, female, and womb contents, placing the section's desert animal and sex vocabulary in the same scene.
Embryonic stages in wombs and barren earth that stirs, swells, and grows every delightful pair after rain make human gestation and fertile soil interpret each other.
The Creator makes pairs in what the earth grows, in human beings, and beyond their knowledge, directly supporting the section's extension of male and female into cultivated ground.
The good tree تُؤْتِىٓ أُكُلَهَا every season by its Lord's permission, joining the section's itāʾ as fruiting, growth, and dependence on Rabb.
Both gardens give their full produce without withholding anything, a concrete Quranic use of آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا for the fruit-bearing sense attached to يُؤْتِى in the source section.
Water descends from the sky for drink and produces the vegetation in which livestock graze, joining cloud, pasture, and herd in a single causal scene.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, supplying the plant increase and date yield behind the section's paired verbs of giving and growing.
The question أَفَرَءَيْتُم مَّا تَحْرُثُونَ fixes attention on the human act of sowing that precedes, but does not cause, growth.
The next question asks whether people cause the seed to grow or God does, sharply assigning the section's growth to the true nurturer.
The mockers target both voluntary almsgivers and those who find only their own effort to give; the latter embody the section's giver who comes by his own striving instead of waiting for collection.
The wealthy and constrained are each commanded to spend from what God gave, and the ayah promises ease after hardship; spending and the y-s-r branch meet in an economic setting.
Male and female almsgivers who lend God a good loan have it multiplied, expressing charitable giving as increase rather than depletion.
People do not attain birr until they spend from what they love, paralleling 22:37's distinction between the material object offered and the inward quality that truly reaches God.
Believers must spend from their good earnings and from what God brings out of the earth, directly linking acceptable giving to agricultural produce.
Giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is declared best for those seeking God's face, matching both the harvest-right and face-seeking motives of the section.
God is the one who accepts repentance and takes charities from His servants, completing the collection scene while shifting its ultimate receiver beyond the human collector.
A recognized share of the giver's wealth belongs to the asker and deprived, corresponding to the crop's due that must be separated at harvest.
The worshippers' wealth contains a known right, making charitable transfer a due within wealth rather than repayment of a private favor.
That known right is for the asker and the deprived, identifying the human destination of the wealth that is given for God.
Those who spend secretly and openly hope for a commerce that will never perish, reversing the apparent loss of wealth in giving.
God fully repays their rewards and increases them from His bounty, supplying divine increase and recompense for the sincere spender.
The command to spend is said to be good for one's own souls, directly matching the section's claim that the giver's purification returns to himself.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, joining charitable expenditure, increase, and cleansing.
Whatever people spend, God replaces it as the best provider, giving the section's non-transactional gift a divine rather than human return.
A debtor in hardship receives delay until ease, while waiving the debt as charity is better; financial ʿusr/yusr and voluntary release of what is owed meet in one ayah.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ closely repeats the promise-form and destination of 92:7, while the same surah later names the one who purifies himself.
After the successful person purifies himself in 87:14, he remembers his Lord's name and prays; this gives that purification its Godward orientation, as 92:20 does.
The sacred state, sacrificial animals, and their garlands must not be violated, confirming هدي as a visible class of animals directed to the sanctuary.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are appointed as supports for people, again joining the sanctuary to hady livestock.
In the sacrificial-animal passage, the humble fear when God is named, endure, pray, and spend from His provision; this supplies the piety and giving that 22:37 says reach God.
God makes the earth serviceable, sends rain, and brings out diverse pairs of plants, uniting fit soil, cloud, paired vegetation, and divine nurture.
People eat those plants and pasture their livestock in them, completing 20:53's rain-and-growth scene with the herd.
Winds announce mercy and pure water descends from the sky, providing the cloud-borne source of the section's plant nurture.
That water revives dead land and gives drink to abundant livestock and humans, directly joining pasture-making rain to the herd it sustains.
The entire sequence of water, split earth, grain, palms, and pasture is finally named provision for people and their livestock, stating the meeting that the section develops.
A dead field is revived and grain is brought out for people to eat, presenting agricultural growth as a divine life-giving sign.
Gardens of date palms and grapes with flowing springs supply the exact fruit-bearing landscape behind the section's itāʾ and zakā imagery.
People eat the fruit although their hands did not create it, setting received provision against any self-sufficient claim to growth.
Rain produces every plant, grain, date clusters, grapes, olives, and pomegranates, and the reader is told to observe fruiting and ripening; it is a full scene of cloud-grown yield.
God sends rain and grows splendid gardens whose trees humans could not grow, directly assigning the crop's nurture to the Lord.
Water is driven to barren land and brings out crops eaten by both livestock and people, closely matching the section's joined herd-and-field economy.
Some desert Arabs treat expenditure as nearness to God and a means to the Messenger's prayers, embodying the sincere alternative to payment regarded as a levy.
Food is given despite love for it to the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9 then states that this materially costly gift seeks only God's face.
Spenders who do not follow gifts with reminders of favor or injury receive their reward with God, clarifying what it means to give without establishing a human debt.
Concealed alms reach the poor and expiate wrongs, giving charitable transfer an explicit cleansing effect.
Birr includes giving loved wealth to vulnerable people alongside prayer and zakat, making costly transfer of māl a substantive sign of truthfulness and piety.
A good loan to God is multiplied many times, another direct formulation of giving that grows with God.
The one who lends God a good loan receives it multiplied and a noble reward, aligning increase with a Godward gift rather than a human repayment.
Money advanced to grow in people's wealth does not grow with God, whereas zakat given seeking His face is multiplied; this is the section's exact boundary between apparent and real increase.
Good land brings out vegetation by its Lord's permission while bad land yields only meagerly, a direct boundary between fit soil and coarse or unfruitful growth.
A showy gift followed by reminders or injury is soil on bare rock: rain strips it clean, the precise failed-rain counterpart to the fruitful garden of 2:265.
God effaces usury and causes charities to grow, making the two opposed kinds of increase in the section an explicit divine contrast.
Humans are known even as embryos in their mothers' wombs and therefore must not declare themselves pure; womb, taqwa, and the boundary on self-purification meet in one ayah.
Those who pronounce themselves pure are corrected: God purifies whom He wills, defining the divine boundary around the source section's self-purifying verb.
No one would ever become pure without God's grace and mercy; this guards the agricultural metaphor from making the giver the independent cause of his own growth.
Those summoned to spend who act stingily are stingy only against themselves, the direct inverse of giving that purifies and benefits its giver.
The one who buries or corrupts the soul fails, furnishing the immediate opposite to the purifier who flourishes in 91:9.
A productive palm-and-grape garden is destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is most vulnerable, making the loss of accumulated yield a warning beside the multiplying garden of 2:265.
The owners of a garden are tested after resolving to harvest it at dawn, opening a sustained reversal of the section's crop-giver scene.
They make their harvest oath without qualification, exposing the self-sufficient stance later corrected by the Lord's destruction of the crop.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, assigning the failure of expected yield to the power beyond the cultivators.
The garden becomes like a dark, stripped field, the visual opposite of the crop that increases and gives fruit.
The owners call one another early, beginning the deliberate attempt to secure the harvest for themselves.
They hurry to harvest if they are going to cut the crop, fixing the episode at the same moment when 6:141 commands that the crop's right be given.
They set out whispering together, showing that exclusion from the harvest is planned rather than accidental.
Their stated purpose is that no poor person enter the garden that day, a direct reversal of giving the crop's due at harvest.
They go out convinced of their power to withhold, opposing the giver who recognizes yield as the Lord's provision.
On seeing the ruined garden they first think they have lost the way, registering how completely expected abundance has vanished.
They realize that they have been deprived, the crop analogue of the source section's milk expected to continue but suddenly cut off.
The most balanced owner asks why they did not glorify God, restoring the Lordward stance absent from their harvest plan.
They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, belatedly acknowledging the true nurturer of the garden.
They name themselves transgressors after intending to deny the poor, exposing the moral failure behind the barren field.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better and turn their desire toward Him, reversing self-reliant possession after the crop's loss.
Two grape gardens ringed by palms and crops begin a parable in which abundant yield becomes the setting for false confidence in wealth.
The owner boasts that he exceeds his companion in wealth and people, joining agricultural fruit to the māl whose imagined sufficiency the section denies.
He enters his garden wronging himself and says it will never perish, echoing the expectation of continued yield behind the section's prematurely failing milk.
His companion says he should have acknowledged God's will and power on entering the garden, locating increase under the Lord rather than the owner.
The companion expects his Lord may give him a better garden and send a calamity upon the boaster's, setting divine gift against possessed yield.
The garden's water may sink beyond recovery, specifying how its continuing growth can be cut off.
The fruit is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent while the trellises lie fallen, making wealth and crop fail together.
No group can help the owner apart from God and he cannot help himself, corresponding to wealth that cannot avail when its owner falls.
The episode ends by locating true protection and the best outcome with God, restoring the Lord as the source and end of increase.
When the people of Saba turn away, the flood replaces their two gardens with bitter, sparse growth, a large-scale reversal of blessed crop increase.
The ruined yield is identified as recompense for ingratitude, connecting lost provision with failure to recognize the giver.
A corrupt word is an uprooted tree with no stability, the barren inverse of the fruitful tree that gives by its Lord's permission.
Rain-swollen vegetation is suddenly reaped as though it had not flourished the day before, a field-scale parallel to milk mistakenly expected to continue.
Worldly life is vegetation mingled by rain and then scattered dry by winds, sharpening the difference between temporary increase and what remains with the Lord.
Rain becomes varied crops that flourish, yellow, and crumble, making the stages and ending of agricultural increase visible.
Vegetation pleasing its cultivators later withers, yellows, and becomes debris, a boundary against mistaking visible growth of wealth for lasting increase.
Denial of judgment is introduced as the source of a social failure, linking kadhaba to the opposite of truthful giving rather than to words alone.
The denier drives away the orphan, enacting the hard refusal opposed to the section's voluntary giver.
He does not urge feeding the poor, the human consequence of denial set against charity and harvest rights.
Failure to honor the orphan begins a sequence opposing the section's purifying use of wealth.
They do not encourage feeding the poor, reversing the sacrificial and agricultural gift directed to the needy.
They consume inheritance greedily, turning received property inward instead of recognizing a due within it.
Their excessive love of wealth names the attachment overcome by the person who gives his māl to purify himself.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth is the concentrated opposite of one who releases wealth for purification.
He imagines his wealth will make him last, an explicit false confidence in māl like the expectation that yield will never cease.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way embody the withholding opposite to the section's giver.
The hoarded metal is heated and brands their bodies, turning retained wealth into the punishment from which charitable purification would have separated them.
Some promise that if God gives them bounty they will give charity and become righteous, setting up an explicit test of whether received increase will be shared.
When bounty comes they are stingy and turn away, reversing the truthful giver and making the failed promise resemble the section's kadhaba branch.
Some desert Arabs treat expenditure as a punitive liability and await misfortune, the exact motivational opposite of 9:99 and of giving for God's face.
People divide crops and livestock between God and invented partners, a corrupt allocation that exposes why the harvest gift must be directed sincerely to God.
After the surrounding signs of crops and water, people make their response to provision an act of denial, joining rizq to kadhaba in the negative way the section dramatizes.
Blessed rain grows gardens and harvest grain, giving the section's growth a literal source in descending blessing.
Tall date palms with layered clusters specify the fruit-bearing tree behind the source section's dictionary sense of itāʾ as a palm's yield.
The crop is provision for servants and rain revives dead land, completing the movement from blessing to growth and sustenance.
Poured water begins a sequence that ends as provision for people and livestock, so this ayah supplies the rain-source of the joined field-and-herd scene.
The earth is split open before growth, making the prepared ground in the section's fertile-soil imagery concrete.
Grain is grown from the split earth, the basic crop whose increase supports the section's zakat metaphor.
Grapes and fresh fodder appear together, bringing human crop and animal feed into the same agricultural sequence.
Olives and date palms name the tree whose abundant yield the section uses to explain itāʾ.
Dense gardens broaden the productive landscape that rain brings forth.
Fruit and pasture place orchard yield beside the forage needed by the herd.
Winds carry heavy clouds to dead land and rain produces every fruit; it supplies the cloud action whose differing results are judged in 7:58.
Adjoining soils, vineyards, crops, and palms receive one water yet yield differently, a close Quranic elaboration of fit earth and unequal fruitfulness.
Mary's Lord causes her to grow a good growth and entrusts her to care, using plant increase for divinely nurtured human formation much as the section makes the giver a growing tree.
God is said to have grown human beings from the earth as a growth, supporting the section's passage from plant development to human moral increase.
The command to speak of one's Lord's blessing locates niʿma with Rabb, whereas 92:19 denies that the giver acts to repay a human niʿma.
Every blessing people possess is from God, clarifying why the section's gift can bypass human repayment and seek the Lord alone.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, specifying the relational boundary around the unencumbered gift in 2:262-264.
Spending by night and day, secretly and openly, portrays constancy in giving and locates its reward with the Lord.
Private counsel is justified when it orders charity or reconciliation, and action seeking God's pleasure is promised a great reward; motive again distinguishes the gift.
Believers are told to spend from God's provision before a day when exchange and human alliances cannot operate, relating present giving to wealth's future inability to avail.
Prayer and secret or open spending are commanded before a day without trade or friendship, another specific boundary between transferable wealth now and useless wealth later.
Those who prefer others despite their own need and are guarded from selfish greed enact the non-reciprocal generosity of the section's giver.
Spending in both ease and hardship shows that giving is not merely the overflow of abundance, a useful boundary for the source section's yusr imagery.
The dying person asks for delay in order to give charity and become righteous, showing that wealth must be released voluntarily before its opportunity ends.
A person has only what he strives for, supporting the section's contrast between an external collector and the giver who comes through his own saʿy.
The one who seeks the hereafter, strives for it properly, and believes has his striving thanked; sought end and personal effort are explicitly joined.
The command not to confer a favor seeking increase plausibly marks the same boundary as 92:19-20: a gift is not a claim on a larger human return.
The earth grows every noble pair, a compact parallel to the section's gendered language for productive soil and plants.
God spreads creatures through the earth and grows every noble pair after rain, again joining created pairs to cultivated increase.
The earth contains every kind of fruit in pairs, reinforcing the movement from male and female creation to paired fertility in the field.
A seedling puts out shoots, strengthens, thickens, and stands firm, offering a Quranic scene of gradual completion akin to the section's definition of Rabb's nurture stage by stage.
Rain turns the earth green and is followed by divine gentleness and awareness, a concise scene of growth under God's care.
Humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, and its reviver is identified as the giver of life, assigning fertility beyond the soil itself.
God sends winds, spreads clouds, and releases rain as He wills, spelling out the cloud process presupposed by the section's rabāb image.
The effects of God's mercy are read in His revival of the earth after death, making crop growth a sign of the giver behind it.
Winds raise clouds that God drives to dead land and revives with rain, another full cloud-to-field enactment of nurture.
Measured water revives a dead land, linking provision in due measure to the field's restored capacity to grow.
Abundant water poured from rain clouds starts a concise sequence of grain, plants, and gardens.
The rain brings forth grain and vegetation, the crop increase at the center of the section's zakat image.
Dense gardens complete the rain-grown sequence as a scene of abundant yield.
God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it, presenting the provision that sustains the herd.
Water and pasture are explicitly enjoyment for people and their livestock, matching the two beneficiaries joined throughout the section.
The reader is made to consider the water people drink, shifting attention from possessed provision to its source.
The question asks whether humans send water down from the rain cloud or God does, a direct correction to independent claims over the source of growth.
God could make that water bitter, setting a boundary on the apparently secure provision that feeds fields and herds.
The Creator of all pairs also provides ships and livestock for riding, joining paired creation and herd utility as the section does.
Riders are told to remember their Lord's blessing when settled on their mounts, turning useful livestock into acknowledgment of niʿma.
The rider confesses the return to the Lord, redirecting the animal's benefit from possession toward its ultimate giver.
Livestock include burden-bearers and smaller animals, and people may eat God's provision; this adds a Quranic classification of the herd as useful rizq.
People are carried on livestock and ships, continuing 23:21's milk-and-benefit scene with transport.

Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste does not change; this may offer a deliberately lasting milk-image against the source section's lexicographic milk that was expected to last but failed, though the ayah speaks of quality rather than supply.
